title: US Proposal to End the 60-Day Grace Period: Implications for H-1B and High-Skilled Mobility
fullText:
CURRENT AFFAIRS 207
US Proposal to End the 60-Day Grace Period: Implications for H-1B
and High-Skilled Mobility
Category
GS
Date
Quick rule
International Relations / Diaspora
GS II
12 Sep 2026
Read highlighted facts first
FAST READ - read only this box if short on time
• The US Department of Homeland Security proposed removing the discretionary up-to-60-day grace period available
after job loss to several non-immigrant worker categories, including H-1B.
• The grace period was created in the 2016 AC21 final rule and became effective in January 2017.
• Any change can affect job mobility, immigration status risk and Indian high-skilled professionals in the United States.
WHY IN NEWS
• The proposal directly affects the resilience of employment-based migration by reducing the time available to find a new
sponsor or otherwise regularise status after job loss.
• For India, it is relevant to diaspora welfare, skilled mobility, services trade and bilateral economic ties.
TOP DATA & FACTS
• DHS published the proposed rule on 11 September 2026.
• The proposal concerns 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
• The existing provision allows an up-to-60-day discretionary grace period after cessation of employment.
• Covered categories include H-1B and several other employment-based non-immigrant classifications.
• The grace period is discretionary rather than an automatic 60-day entitlement in every case.
• It was established by the 2016 AC21 final rule.
• The rule became effective on 17 January 2017.
• Its purpose included job portability, stability and flexibility for high-skilled workers.
• Loss of status can affect ability to extend or change status.
• H-1B is an employer-linked non-immigrant work classification.
• A proposed rule is not the same as a final rule.
• Notice-and-comment rulemaking permits public participation before finalisation.
• Indian professionals form a major constituency in US high-skilled migration.
• Migration rules can affect firms' ability to move talent across borders.
• Skilled mobility is also relevant to trade in services and innovation networks.

PRELIMS
• H-1B is a US non-immigrant classification.
• The 60-day period is discretionary and linked to cessation of employment.
• A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking does not itself equal a final binding rule.
• US administrative rulemaking commonly includes notice and comment.
• Employer sponsorship shapes H-1B mobility.
• Immigration policy can have economic and bilateral effects beyond border control.
QUICK REVISION
Key distinction: proposal versus final rule. Remember 2016 AC21 rule -> effective 2017 -> up to 60 days after job loss ->
2026 DHS proposal to remove the provision. Link to diaspora, services, talent mobility and legal-status risk.
PROBABLE OBJECTIVE QUESTION
With reference to the above topic, consider the following statements:
1. The existing grace period can be up to 60 days after cessation of employment.
2. The 2026 DHS document is a proposed rule rather than a final rule.
3. H-1B is an immigrant visa that automatically grants permanent residence.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3
Answer: (a) 1 and 2 only
Explanation: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. H-1B is a non-immigrant employment classification and does not automatically
confer permanent residence.

PROBABLE MAINS QUESTION
Changes in destination-country work-visa rules can become a foreign-policy and economic issue for India. Discuss with
reference to high-skilled mobility and the proposed US H-1B grace-period change.
MODEL ANSWER - ~300 WORDS
INTRODUCTION
The proposal directly affects the resilience of employment-based migration by reducing the time available to find a new
sponsor or otherwise regularise status after job loss. Any change can affect job mobility, immigration status risk and
Indian high-skilled professionals in the United States.
SIGNIFICANCE
• High-skilled mobility supports technology, services trade and innovation networks.
• A transition period after job loss reduces abrupt status insecurity.
• Predictable rules help firms and workers plan cross-border careers.
CHALLENGES
• Tighter transition rules can increase worker vulnerability and employer dependence.
• Frequent policy changes create uncertainty for households and businesses.
• India has limited control over another country's domestic immigration law.
WAY FORWARD
• Strengthen consular information and legal-awareness support for affected Indians.
• Diversify global mobility partnerships and expand domestic high-skill opportunities.
• Use bilateral dialogue to communicate the economic value of predictable talent mobility.
Because the proposal is not yet a final rule, policy analysis must distinguish consultation from implementation. Employers, universities, immigration lawyers and affected workers may submit comments during the rulemaking process, and the final text could change. This distinction matters for public communication so that Indian professionals do not make costly decisions based on a proposal being reported as an already-operative legal requirement.

CONCLUSION
The episode shows that migration regulation is also economic infrastructure: small legal changes can materially alter
labour mobility, bargaining power and bilateral talent flows.
The practical effect of removing the grace period would depend on the final rule, effective date and any transition
provisions. Workers facing sudden termination could have less time to secure a new petition, change status or depart,
increasing the importance of rapid legal advice and employer compliance. Indian technology firms and professionals
should track the rulemaking process rather than treating the proposal as already operative. Consular outreach can
explain status risks, while bilateral economic engagement can emphasise how predictable mobility supports innovation
and investment on both sides.
